blogs.content: Don’t Call It a Decision Model - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Thoughts Thoughts Don’t Call It a Decision Model Nov 3, 2026 Nov 3, 2026 Nov 3, 2026 Jev makes judgments , code makes decisions . Allie Laabs, DevRel, TypeSafe We love that people have recognized the importance of the new category of models that Jev pioneered. It’s unsurprising that the term “decision models” has caught on as a name. When you first see Jev pick an option from a list, it’s easy to see it as making decisions. And indeed, we have used the word “decision” in our own education materials! So why is TypeSafe holding firm on calling Jev a System One model instead of a decision model? Let’s talk about it. The System One name comes from the concept Daniel Kahneman popularized in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow . System 1 thinking is fast and intuitive. System 2 is slower and more deliberate. With Jev, the emphasis is on fast, focused judgments, hence the System One name. It’s about where Jev fits in a system Let’s break down what a typical system is, using the metaphor of circuits: inputs on the left (your data, application state, etc), they flow into logic, and then outputs on the right. Let’s use a simplified version of the Customer Service workflow from our evals page as an example. The naive approach to using Jev in this workflow would be to place the entire decision in to a single Jev question: When people first see Jev, this is how they imagine it fitting in to systems: give it all of your state, and have it make a decision about what should happen . This often looks like one big Choice question, and stuffing lots of semantic descriptions of business logic and caveats in to the criteria field. While this can work, you will quickly find yourself engaging in what we call prompt gymnastics : tweaking these long explanations of conditions over and over to get each edge case handled. And then the next day you get some input you hadn’t thought of, the system fails, and you’re back to stuffing more caveats and clarifications in to criteria prose. What’s happening here is trying to put intelligence at the wrong layer of abstraction. Your system already knows the criteria for each of your expected outcomes, and only some of it actually requires judgement. The rest is cold, hard logic: When Exit reports an unauthorized charge Fraud team: freeze & dispute asks for a person, or threatens legal action Hand to a person wants money back, claim eligible, ≤ $25 Refund now wants money back, claim eligible, over $25 Refunds team reviews wants to cancel, subscription active, open to an offer Offer to stay otherwise Answer & continue So where does Jev fit in to this kind of system? To understand the answer, we need to peek inside to see what a decision is actually made of: Peel off the cap Decisions in a system are rarely one atomic choice. Peel off the cap and we find wires running from the inputs through nodes of code and nodes of judgment . Decisions in software, workflows, and business are built this way. Checking “claim eligible, unpaid” is math. Answering “does the user want money back?” takes judgment. That’s where Jev belongs, and it’s exactly what we mean by System One: the quick intuitive judgments a knowledgeable person makes in seconds. Code is great for answering what it can answer exactly. Jev answers only the small questions code can’t. Logic then combines those answers into the decision. It’s the combination of both judgement and code that allows a system to make reliable, observable decisions. Why Build It This Way 1. Clarity of design Reliable systems require a clear understanding of how decisions are made. blogs.content: Technical Building Ethical Wall Enforcement Into Harvey How we bring a firm’s matter restrictions into document access, search, and AI work. by Shuaiwei Cui , Lilly Xia , and Nick Howlett • Nov 13, 2026 Imagine a lawyer using Harvey to analyze documents for Acme Corporation’s confidential acquisition. A colleague is barred from accessing information about the deal. That restriction must also apply to conversations and other work created from those documents, even if someone shares the work with the colleague. Law firms organize work around matters, such as a deal, lawsuit, or advisory engagement. An ethical wall, also called an information barrier, limits who can access information about a matter. An inclusionary wall allows access only to people on its list; an exclusionary wall blocks the people on its list and allows everyone else in. Bringing ethical walls into an AI platform means protecting information wherever it is used. Firms manage matter records and wall policies in their own systems, and Harvey imports them. A document management system (DMS) enforces walls on the documents it stores. But Harvey also creates conversations, tables, and drafts from those documents. Because that work lives in Harvey, our platform must enforce the walls on it too. To do that, Harvey links resources — including Vault projects and files, conversations, and Review Tables — to Client Matters and their walls. This creates three engineering challenges: Import matters and walls reliably, at the scale of a large firm Help people find the matters they can access Enforce walls the same way across different kinds of work The rest of the blog explains the architecture Harvey uses to carry each firm’s ethical wall rules across the platform, from the matter model to the safeguards around wall data. Figure 1. Harvey imports matters and walls from firm systems. On every request, it checks both resource permission and matter clearance. Importing Client Matters and Walls Before Harvey can enforce a wall, it needs the matter and its policy. Our import architecture separates matter identity from access policy. Provider adapters translate data from each wall provider into one common model. Each firm’s data stays in its own workspace, the firm’s private Harvey environment. Two separate sync jobs We split import into two jobs. Client Matter sync finds matters in the external system and links each one to an existing Harvey Client Matter or creates a new one. When walls are enabled, it can also set up the matter’s wall. Wall sync refreshes the policy for matters already linked to the external system. It fetches each matter’s current policy, matches the people on it to Harvey users, applies membership changes, and updates whether the matter is open or walled. We keep these jobs separate for three reasons: Each job can run on its own schedule. A firm opens new matters at a steady pace, but a wall can change at any moment, for example when a lateral hire arrives with a conflict. Wall sync can run on demand without a scan of the full matter catalog. A failure in one job does not block the other. If a wall fetch fails for one matter, matter import continues. If matter import stalls, existing walls still refresh. Firms do not have to adopt both at once. Matter data and wall data often live in different systems. A firm can bring its matters into Harvey before it turns on walls, or without walls at all. For supported integrations, Client-Matter-only sync links an imported document collection to its matter in Vault, even if the firm has not set up walls in Harvey. The project is filed under the right matter from the start. Figure 2. Import architecture. Matter sync and wall sync are separate jobs. Each runs on a recurring schedule, as a one-time bulk run, or for a single matter. Recurring and ad hoc execution Durable workflows run bulk syncs. blogs.content: Alyssa Levy works with some of the smallest legal teams Legora serves, and some of the fastest-moving. As a Go-to-market (GTM) Associate on Legora's small and medium-sized business (SMB) team in New York, she works with solo practitioners, boutique law firms, mid-sized firms and in-house legal teams. For many of these teams, the entire legal department is just one lawyer. Their industries and practice areas vary. What they share is a small, agile team with more work than hours, and a need to move faster. Legora helps them do it. Many of the teams Alyssa works with assume Legora is built exclusively for larger teams. One question she hears time and again is: “How many seats do we have to buy?” Her answer is simple. “You can start with just one,” she says. “There’s no minimum number of seats. We build the package around the team you have today, with room to grow.” Alyssa Levy's path to small legal teams Alyssa joined Legora as a business development representative (BDR). Before that, she worked across editorial writing, startup marketing and investing. She studied Organizational Studies and History at the University of Michigan. As a BDR, her job was to start conversations and earn a few minutes of a busy lawyer's time. Today she runs the full cycle with small and mid-sized teams, from the first call through the trial to signature. “Being a BDR taught me to respect people's time,” she says. “That matters even more with small teams. The partner at a five-person firm is often also the one handling billing, hiring and the client work.” What keeps her in SMB is how directly the work lands. “When a small team gets time back, they feel it that same week,” she says. “There's no rollout committee between the product and the person using it.” What small legal teams get from Legora Alyssa's clients include boutique law firms, mid-sized firms and lean in-house teams. Many of the in-house teams she works with are one or two lawyers handling requests from across the business. The work differs from team to team. The constraint is the same: more matters than hours, and no spare headcount to absorb the difference. “My clients don't have an innovation team or a knowledge management function,” she says. “They want what a large firm has, without the large-firm overhead. Legora gives them that at the size they are today.” For in-house teams, that often means keeping work in-house that used to go to outside counsel. For boutiques, it means taking on more without adding headcount. It starts with how teams buy. Legora has no seat minimum and no license floor, so a team can start with one license and grow from there. Legora works with each team directly to find the pricing package that fits its timeline, needs and budget, starting with a short consultation. How small legal teams move faster Small teams don't need a long evaluation to know whether something works. Alyssa can usually see it during the trial. Word Add-in, Skills, playbooks and Tabular Review “When a team turns on the Word Add-in or starts building Skills, I know Legora is becoming part of how they work,” she says. “Anything where they create something that automates work they do over and over, like a repeatable workflow or a playbook, is a huge value add. When I see a team running thousands of cells in Tabular Review , I know it's working for them.” In plain terms, the Word Add-in brings Legora into Microsoft Word, Skills are reusable instructions that teach Legora how a team completes a task, a playbook records a team's standards for work it repeats, and Tabular Review runs the same questions across many documents and shows the answers in a table. blogs.description: Connect Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Calendar to the Legora Agent, and bring the documents, conversations, and schedules behind your legal work into Legora.
blogs.content: Today, we’re making Google Workspace generally available in Legora, so the tools you already use every day can now support your legal work. Legal work spans more than the documents you're reviewing. Agreements live in shared drives, important decisions are captured in email conversations, and meetings keep matters moving. That information provides essential context, but bringing it together often means searching across applications and manually moving files. With Google Workspace connected, the Legora Agent can work directly with information across Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Calendar. Find documents, understand the correspondence behind an agreement, and manage meetings, all through the Agent. Bring your documents and conversations together The Agent can search Google Drive for agreements, policies, and other files, and bring them into Legora for review and analysis. Instead of downloading documents and uploading them manually, you can ask the Agent to find what you need. But the document is often only part of the story. Important details about an agreement may sit in the emails exchanged around it. With Gmail connected, the Agent can find relevant conversations and attachments, helping you understand what was discussed, what was agreed, and how a negotiation developed. You can also work across both sources. Ask the Agent to find an agreement in Drive, retrieve the related correspondence in Gmail, and combine that information to work from. From understanding the work to moving it forward Google Workspace also extends what the Agent can help you do next. Ask the Agent to draft an email response informed by the correspondence you've reviewed, ready for you to approve and send or save as a draft. With Google Calendar connected, the Agent can check availability, find a suitable meeting time, and create or update events with your approval. These capabilities bring more of the everyday work surrounding a legal matter into Legora, from finding the relevant information to coordinating the next step. Getting started with Google Workspace Google Workspace is available through a single connection, with administrators controlling which services are enabled for their organization. Administrators enable the Google Workspace integration under Settings → Features → Integrations, choosing which services to make available across Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Calendar. Users connect their Google account under Settings → Personal → Connectors → Google Workspace and begin working with the enabled services through the Agent. The integration respects each user's existing Google permissions, so the Agent can only access information the user is authorized to see. Actions that send emails or change files or calendar events require user approval. For more information on configuring the integration, visit our Google Workspace setup guide .

blogs.content: Product Close Contracts Faster With Every Version in One Place Contract Intelligence brings every round of negotiation into one place, so teams reach agreement faster and learn from every deal. by Harvey Team • Nov 12, 2026 The latest redline rarely tells the whole story of a negotiation. It shows what changed since the last draft, but not why earlier terms were accepted or what Legal conceded to get them. That context is scattered across email threads and earlier drafts, so Legal has to retrace past decisions to see whether a new change reopens something they already negotiated. With the latest updates to Contract Intelligence , the full deal history stays with the contract, so you can assess risk in context and move every contract to signature faster. You can pick up each new round with prior versions and related agreements in view, track progress through to signature, and draw on signed agreements to inform future reviews. Every round builds on the last, and every signed deal strengthens the next. Watch Video Pick Up Where the Last Round Left Off Consider an in-house lawyer negotiating a software vendor’s master services agreement and order form. The vendor returns a new markup after Legal has already agreed to some terms, and the lawyer needs to see what changed and how it compares to what’s already been agreed. If the original reviewer is out, whoever picks up the review needs that same context to keep the deal moving. Contract Intelligence keeps that history with the contract. It matches the new version to the existing contract and adds it to the overview alongside prior rounds and related agreements. Harvey then reviews the new round in context, accounting for positions Legal already accepted. Any lawyer on the team can go straight to the open points that need their judgment, and decide how to respond with confidence. Know Where Every Contract Stands Once the lawyer sends the redline back, the next question is where the deal stands. Across a busy contracting queue, that can mean spending time chasing reviewers or updating a separate spreadsheet to get an answer. With contract statuses, Legal and Legal Ops can see which agreements are in review, which are waiting on the counterparty, and which are signed. When the business asks for an update, the team has one place to check. When a deadline approaches, they can see which contracts still need attention. Put Signed Agreements to Work Once the contract is signed, it goes into your repository where the terms Legal accepted are extracted to inform future reviews. On the next vendor agreement, Contract Review Agents can draw on those signed positions to inform its redline suggestions, and Legal can see how past negotiations played out when deciding where to hold firm and where there may be room to move. Teams can also ask Harvey direct questions about their agreements, such as “Which vendors pushed back on our data security terms, and what did we accept?” “ The proof is in the name. The intelligence, the data, the insights will drive some great discussions. I had intuition, but I didn't always have the data to back me up. So being able to get that data and discuss it with the business in a way they can relate to is really exciting to me. ” Kelley Williams Associate GC at Koch The judgment that goes into a negotiation should keep helping the team after signature. With Contract Intelligence, each review builds on the last so teams reach agreement faster. Today, she takes on an expanded role at Legora, leading our work with governments and public agencies, starting in the UK and EMEA. blogs.content: Lucy Frazer KC has seen the pressures on public institutions from the inside. A former Cabinet minister and twice Solicitor General, she served in six government departments, with ministerial roles across courts, prisons, probation, legal services and criminal law. Today she takes on an expanded role at Legora, leading our work with governments and public agencies, starting in the UK and EMEA. We asked Lucy about what she saw during her time in government, why she chose Legora, and what public bodies should expect from any AI supplier before they can trust it. Which experiences in government most shaped how you think about the pressures on the public sector for those working in law, or law adjacent areas? Government and public agencies face many challenges. Cases collapsing because of incorrect disclosure. Decisions in immigration cases being judicially reviewed because a step in the process had been missed. And significant backlogs in our courts. I saw first-hand how the pressures on government were growing: the explosion of evidence in criminal cases, the rise in cases coming through our courts, and an overstretched prison system. In government, we were looking to technology to bring new answers to old problems. In the NHS, for example, da Vinci robotic-assisted surgery was helping patients with prostate cancer, and predictive analysis was being used to bring down waiting lists. It was obvious to me that technology could fundamentally change every area of government, including the justice system. What did you see in Legora that persuaded you to take on a bigger role with the company ? Three things matter to me: I want to work for a company that is bringing about positive societal benefits through AI. I want a can-do, positive culture, with dynamic leadership driving that change. And I want a company that truly works in partnership with its clients, listening to their needs and building its products on feedback and collaboration. I see all of this at Legora. Its tools can fundamentally change the delivery of legal and legal-adjacent public services. Tools for legal research and factual analysis save significant time and cost, and more broadly they can bring order to disorder in the management of legal processes. Its operating model relies on legal engineers, lawyers who work alongside the technical teams, so there is a real culture of collaboration with clients. Under Max’s incredible leadership, Legora has come further, faster, than any company in legal technology. In a very short time, it has built a brand that law firms recognise and trust. We want that same collaborative model to extend into the public sector, working in partnership with government to solve the problems it faces in delivering better, more streamlined services to citizens. What are the biggest obstacles to modernising the justice system with technology, and what would give decision makers the confidence to move faster? Many of our departments have legacy IT systems and those that work within government are understandably concerned about change and how to implement that change. We need to remind ourselves that not embracing technology also brings significant risk. What gives decision makers confidence is seeing it work for themselves. I would recommend that any public body tries a supplier before it buys. Legora included. For the public sector, we say that trust is not a differentiator; it’s a precondition. You’ve said the public sector needs to be confident in the AI it adopts. What does a public body need to see from a supplier before it can trust it? The judiciary’s own guidance on AI sets a good benchmark: AI can support the work but must never make the decision, and every output has to be checked. blogs.content: Product How Legal Engineers Would Use Harvey Agents for Outlook Harvey Legal Engineers, all former practicing lawyers, draw on their experience to show how Harvey can help manage their emails and calendars, giving them more time for substantive legal work. by Harvey Team • Nov 12, 2026 Legal work often begins in an inbox, whether it’s a client question, a court notice, comments on a draft, or documents for a deal. Each message can prompt a series of small tasks: what needs review, who should follow up, and where correspondence belongs. Those tasks keep matters moving, but managing them can take time from substantive legal work, especially when lawyers are receiving hundreds of emails a day. Unlike generic AI assistants, Harvey is built for the legal work that lands in someone’s inbox. Harvey Agents for Outlook can work across a single email or your entire inbox, acting as your legal AI assistant to handle recurring tasks. Harvey can prepare a tailored daily briefing highlighting priorities, draft emails using team knowledge, create tasks, and organize correspondence and attachments in Vault . Lawyers review and approve each action, keeping key decisions in their hands while reducing the manual steps around them In this post, Harvey Legal Engineers — former lawyers who have managed busy inboxes themselves — share where these agents could have helped in their day-to-day work. Start the Day With a Clear View of Priorities Maria Paz Lestido ’s ongoing casework included arbitration matters, with steady correspondence from clients, partners, and co-counsel, as well as regular check-ins and team meetings. She started her day on her phone, prioritizing emails from key clients and partners, then messages addressed directly to her or where she was tagged. She flagged anything important or immediately due. During hearings, she sometimes only had time to skim her inbox and organize messages later. An agent could have helped Maria Paz keep track of the emails competing for her attention, especially on hearing days. In Outlook, a scheduled Harvey Agent can prepare a tailored briefing that summarizes the day’s meetings, highlights emails requiring a response, and flags outstanding follow-ups. It can also recommend calendar changes and draft events for review and approval. With an agent like this, Maria Paz could easily see what needed attention first, what could be delegated, and what could wait, without worrying that she’d missed something. That inbox-and-calendar connection also mattered in Lisa Pagel ’s in-house litigation work at a large insurance company, where she received court orders and emails from opposing counsel with dates for hearings, depositions, and other appearances. She reviewed messages one by one, then had to make sure each date and its relevant details made it onto her calendar. That could mean coordinating reporters, counsel, videographers, and locations with up to 15 people. An agent could surface those messages in her briefing and draft calendar events for her to review against the rest of her schedule. Kick Off New Work With the Right Context Former M&A attorney Shelton Oliver typically worked across six or seven matters at once, and her inbox could become chaotic, especially near signing and closing. It filled with comments from specialist teams and partners, documents from the other side, and questions and feedback from clients. blogs.content: Two years into my career as a disputes lawyer at a leading City firm, I asked myself a question that changed everything: what makes a successful partner in ten years' time? The answer is not more billable hours, a narrower specialism, or a bigger contacts book. The successful partners of the future will be those who have learned to leverage technology so completely that it has fundamentally altered who they are as lawyers - not just the speed at which they work, but the quality of their thinking, the breadth of what they can take on, and the value they deliver to clients. I realised that the lawyers who would thrive were not the ones dabbling in AI. The lawyers who would thrive were rebuilding their entire practice around it. That realisation set me on a path from practising law to helping build the technology I'd become obsessed with. But this piece isn't about me. It's about you - and the mental model shift that will separate the lawyers who thrive in 2030 from those who get left behind. Use cases are just the beginning As a Legal Engineer, a large part of my role involves running use case discovery sessions with the lawyers who use the Legora platform. The objective is straightforward: diagnose friction points in a lawyer's practice, identify which ones AI can address, and build solutions accordingly. These sessions are truly valuable. They give lawyers who are new to AI a concrete starting point, a reason to engage, and real momentum. But here's what I've observed: for many lawyers, use cases become the ceiling rather than the floor. They attend a session, compile a list of four or five things the tool is good for, and then reach for AI only when one of those scenarios arises. Document review? Sure. Issues list from an SPA? Absolutely. But everything else continues exactly as before - the same processes, the same bottlenecks, the same way of practising law that hasn't materially changed in decades. Use cases are the perfect on-ramp. The problem is when lawyers treat them as the destination. This is the classic faster horse problem. When Henry Ford asked people what they wanted, they said a faster horse. They couldn't conceive of the car because they were trapped in the mental model of what already existed. And that is exactly what is happening in law right now. We are retrofitting old ways of working onto a technology that demands an entirely new operating model. We're trying to bolt a jet engine onto a horse-drawn carriage and wondering why it doesn't fly. My time in practice When my previous firm rolled out Legora, I threw myself into it - not tentatively, not with a list of approved use cases, but completely. My mindset was simple: whenever a new piece of work came in, I would assume that the platform could help. I would open it before I even knew how I was going to use it. I wasn't deterred when it took time to figure out the right approach. I treated every task as an opportunity to push the boundaries of what was possible. Within months, Legora was the first thing I opened in the morning and the last thing I closed at night. It wasn't a tool I reached for occasionally. It was my legal operating system: the place where all of my work lived, where every document, every matter, every piece of context was connected and accessible. Agentic systems, which were not available to me in practice, elevate this dramatically, reducing the onus on lawyers to know and select the right tool, and shifting their role to that of direction, supervision, critical analysis, and as the ultimate arbiter of what work leaves the building. And of course I would, but if we're having a prompt-sharing exercise, we are in danger of missing the point. Each statement of work (SOW) signed under it adds the scope, deliverables, and fees for one project. An MSA review is the legal review of those master terms before signature, and because SOWs usually inherit them, it also sets the rules for SOWs nobody has drafted yet. Take a hypothetical MSA your company is about to sign with an IT services provider. SOW-1 for implementation ($1.2 million) and SOW-3 for support ($300,000, billed annually in advance) are signed with the MSA. SOW-2, a $40,000 migration of customer personal data, follows four months later. All figures in this example are illustrative. Ten months after the MSA is signed, partway through SOW-2, a breach exposes the migrated customer data and leads to a $2 million claim against the provider. Whether the cap limits that claim to $40,000 or leaves room for all of it turns on a few words in the MSA's limitation of liability. Those words get settled during the MSA review, months before SOW-2 is written. We’ll follow this MSA from the provider’s first draft to the SOW-2 signature and show where legal AI helps. The Cap Definition Decides Whether a $2 Million Claim Gets Limited to $40,000 The provider's draft caps its liability at the fees paid or payable under "the applicable SOW" in the 12 months before the claim. That reads as standard until you run it against SOW-2, the smallest SOW and the one carrying customer data. blogs.content: Insights Find Every Auto Renewal Clause in Your Portfolio Before its Notice Window Closes An auto renewal clause can set a notice deadline months early. Sort contracts by renewal mechanism, map 30 to 180-day windows, and give each one an owner. by Harvey Team • Nov 6, 2026 An auto renewal clause, also called an automatic renewal clause, extends a contract for another term unless a party gives notice by a set deadline. Tracking that deadline on one agreement is simple. A portfolio multiplies the deadlines, and Zylo's 2026 SaaS Management Index found that the average organization manages 211 SaaS renewals annually, before IT services and facilities agreements are counted. Take a hypothetical in-house team with about 400 supplier agreements across SaaS, IT services, and facilities. In this example, 260 of them renew automatically on January 1 unless someone gives notice. Their notice periods run 30, 60, 90, or 180 days, so the deadlines fall anywhere from July 4 to December 1. Reading 400 agreements for the same few renewal facts is the slow part, and AI can take it on. Harvey's review tables pull each agreement's renewal terms into columns linked to the source clause, so the team's time goes to checking those facts and deciding what to renew. We'll follow this team from sorting its contracts to getting each owner's decision in before the notice deadline. An Auto Renewal Clause Extends the Term Unless Someone Gives Notice in Time An automatic renewal clause sets four facts to capture: the renewal term, the notice period, who can give notice, and how notice must be delivered. Here's a sample clause from one of the team's agreements, a $240,000-a-year analytics subscription, written for this example: "This Agreement will renew automatically for successive twelve (12) month renewal terms. Either party may prevent renewal by giving the other written notice of non-renewal at least sixty (60) days before the end of the then-current term. All notices must be delivered to the addresses set out in Section 14.2." Read as data, it gives a 12-month renewal term, a 60-day notice period, a right either party holds, and a delivery rule that points to Section 14.2. A contract auto renewal clause often splits those facts across sections, so the notice address may sit in a general notices clause or in a later amendment. Missing any one of them can leave a notice of non-renewal open to challenge. The Renewal Mechanism Decides Whether Silence Keeps a Contract or Ends it Before any date matters, each contract needs a label for what happens if nobody acts. An auto renewal contract keeps running on silence, while an option to renew lapses on silence, so the two call for opposite actions. blogs.content: Product Introducing Harvey’s Fact Graph for Disputes, Litigation, and Investigations The Harvey fact graph helps disputes, litigation, and investigations teams find and connect facts across millions of documents and build on one evolving record. by Harvey Team • Nov 5, 2026 We’re introducing Harvey’s fact graph, a new capability for disputes, litigation, and investigations teams to find and connect facts across millions of documents. It links those facts to supporting sources, to one another, and to the people, events, and issues they concern—helping teams uncover relationships across the full record over the lifetime of a matter. The fact graph is the newest addition to Harvey Graph , the connected map of legal knowledge and matter context that Harvey’s agents draw on to find the right information, cite it, and carry it forward. From Individual Facts to a Strategic Narrative In litigation and investigation matters, the job is to connect thousands of facts into a strategic narrative: who knew what and when, whether accounts hold up against the evidence, and where the record has gaps. The facts of a matter often seem disconnected, and the work requires ongoing resources to comb through huge volumes of information. An email might show that an executive received a warning about a defect. Meeting notes months later might record their approval of a product launch despite knowledge of the defect. Extracting and connecting those facts helps teams trace actions, assess what the evidence supports, and identify what still needs to be established. Harvey’s fact graph makes those connections across millions of documents, so teams can focus on judgment instead of piecing together the record. It extracts facts from each document, links back to the exact line of text, and connects events across the record, even when related facts seemingly appear disconnected or sit years apart. As new documents are added over time, the fact graph extracts new information, connects it to the existing record, and flags inconsistencies. New evidence or research can fill a gap, challenge an earlier account, or reveal the significance of a detail found months before. Each new document adds to what the team already knows, and the record grows with the matter. Turn Connected Facts Into Work Product Keeping the factual record current is just the foundation. Teams can also carry those facts into chronologies, witness outlines, memos, and reports. Instead of manually updating work product, Harvey keeps the context up-to-date and flags where prior work is outdated. With the fact graph, teams build work product on the same evolving record throughout the life of a matter. Agents in Harvey draw on the facts and connections already established to generate first drafts, from witness interview outlines early in an investigation, to deposition memos as evidence builds, to preparation materials for a hearing or trial. Each stage builds on the team’s accumulated understanding, so no one has to reconstruct the factual context for each new task. Build on Prior Work as Your Matter Progresses Matters can run for years, outlasting the teams that first worked on them. New team members join, responsibilities shift, and new counsel may come in just weeks before trial. Getting up to speed often means reviewing documents again, piecing together earlier analysis, and relying on handoff conversations to understand what the team knows and why. The fact graph keeps the matter’s facts, supporting sources, review decisions, and work product together, so understanding persists through every phase of the matter. Incoming teammates or counsel can easily trace the audit log, see how the team assessed earlier information, and identify inconsistencies. Every member of the team has a starting point that reflects months or years of accumulated work, so they spend less time reconstructing the matter and more time preparing for what comes next. Here’s a closer look at what’s coming to Harvey. Getting there depends on two things: agents that know a matter or project as well as its lawyers do and firms that can govern those agents with confidence. The first is a context problem. Today, many prompts start cold — a lawyer gathers the documents, explains the background, and clarifies every preference. That’s workable for a chat assistant, but it breaks down the moment agents need to carry a matter from one step to the next or when multiple lawyers and agents are collaborating on the project. That’s what Harvey Graph is built for. It maps the relationships across a firm or team’s matter or project, so agents share a map of the work instead of rebuilding it at every step. Instead, firms can offer a common scale for AI fluency that shows students and junior lawyers what firms expect, and gives them a way to prove themselves fluent. by Peter Duffy • Nov 5, 2026 AI fluency is fast becoming a hiring priority for law firms. It means knowing how to use AI effectively in legal work, recognize its limitations, and apply your own judgment to its outputs. For students thinking about recruitment, that raises a practical question: What exactly do firms want students to know regarding AI, and how do you show you’ve got it? A few firms are leading the way with clarity around expectations. One recruitment post I came across recently opened with a single question: “Are you a lawyer who builds?” The post didn't come from a legal tech start-up or an alternative legal service provider, but a newly launched AI-forward practice set up by a leading European law firm. To explain what it meant, the firm pointed candidates to Levels 4 and 5 of Harvey’s recently published AI Fluency Framework : Builders , who create reusable AI tools such as agents and playbooks, and Catalysts , who build for others and set the standards around them. From AI Familiarity to Clear Expectations A few years ago, it would have been unusual to see law firms recruit explicitly for Builders and Catalysts. In the case of the aforementioned recruitment post, the firm made it clear that it needs lawyers who create with AI, not just use it, and it used the framework's levels to outline their expectations. This example shows how the ideal candidate profile has changed and what law firms are looking for specifically — not just an introduction to AI but the ability to build agents and think critically about how and when to use AI, pointing to a clear framework to attain and measure those skills If firms and candidates share a common language for AI fluency, the framework works just as well at the hiring stage as it does for a junior lawyer in development inside the firm. A firm built around AI is likely to be a step ahead of the wider market, but its hiring expectations are an early sign of where recruiting is heading, and quickly. Among the most progressive firms, AI fluency is already a skill set in rising demand. Expectations are getting clearer — and higher. For students, that makes it worth understanding those expectations now, before they become the norm. The Problem With "Comfortable With AI Tools" Look beyond the most AI-forward employers, and the picture is less precise. Many legal job descriptions mention AI in some form: "comfortable with AI tools," "tech-savvy," "keen interest in legal innovation." These phrases signal a firm's intent, but they set a tone without setting a bar. Comfortable doing what? Using AI to summarize a contract, identify key obligations, and check the summary against the source? Using AI to analyze deposition transcripts, identify inconsistencies, and verify findings against the record? Building an agent that teammates or a practice area can rely on, with clear instructions and review steps? Spotting where AI could reshape how a whole team works, then guiding changes to workflows and working practices? These are very different levels of fluency. Today every role can benefit from a clear standard, and for most lawyers that standard should be Proficient : regular, confident use of AI on substantive legal work. Where firms need Builders or Catalysts, being specific matters even more. The same clarity helps throughout a lawyer's career. A shared standard gives interviewers a consistent way to assess AI capability, gives development plans a clear destination, and shows both current and future lawyers what their goals should be, how to develop, and what their next step looks like. Approval matrices often key sign-off to contract value, type, or department. Those gates still decide who approves the deal and who signs, but they say little about who should decide a term that moved away from your standard position. Take a hypothetical customer master services agreement (MSA) worth $400,000 a year, which Sales submits on a Thursday on the customer's paper. The customer asks for a liability cap of 24 months' fees and uncapped indemnity for data breaches. It also wants the right to assign to an acquirer and the right to give notice of non-renewal 60 days before the term ends. Following that MSA from intake to signature shows who approves which term, with what evidence, and on which version. Value Thresholds Decide Who Signs, and Changed Terms Decide Who Approves Them Contract value, contract type, and the contracting entity remain the right triggers for financial and signature gates. A $400,000-a-year deal may need finance approval and a signatory with matching authority even when every term is standard. Those triggers can't tell you who should decide a cap the customer rewrote, so the matrix needs a second dimension keyed to deviations from your playbook. Here's how the MSA's four requests map onto that second dimension: Request in the MSA Status against your playbook Who decides What the decision-maker needs Notice of non-renewal 60 days before the term ends Matches the fallback, since your standard is 90 days and your fallback accepts 60 Contract manager, within delegated authority The fallback rule the request matches Assignment to an acquirer, with no notice Conditional, because the fallback allows it only with written notice Contract manager proposes notice language, and counsel decides if the customer refuses it The fallback, the proposed language, and the customer's response A cap of 24 months' fees Outside the fallback, which stops at 18 months Commercial counsel, within the exception authority your policy gives legal The customer's exact language, your standard and fallback, and prior deals with similar requests Uncapped indemnity for data breaches Shifts risk the business has to own Counsel advises, privacy and insurance stakeholders weigh in, and the CFO, as risk owner for this deal, accepts or rejects the risk The exposure in plain terms, insurance limits, and alternatives such as a separate cap for data-breach claims Two of the four requests can move in a delegated lane once they meet every condition of the fallback, so counsel's exception time goes to the cap and the indemnity. That lane depends on fallbacks legal has written down and formally delegated. Some triggers add a reviewer whatever the deal size, including personal or regulated data, IP ownership, an unfamiliar governing law, insurance requirements, or an unusual contracting entity. Sixty percent of contracts had drafting errors. When a self-driving car crashes, it makes the news. The scrutiny is warranted, but the headlines obscure the baseline. Human drivers cause far more crashes . They happen every day, yet almost none become media stories. In legal work, AI hallucinations also get the headlines. An AI-generated legal brief citing non-existent case studies. A judge who used AI to create a restraining order and misquoted state law. These are real issues that deserve attention. But Spellbook sees a different side to AI’s impact on legal and contract workflow. We see the human mistakes that are made when volume and complexity are met with limited hours and manual review. In fact, our data shows saved hours, greater accuracy and increased output when AI is deployed. So we decided to dig into the data to prove what we already know intuitively—humans make mistakes too. Using Spellbook Reviews, we analyzed 3,000+ SEC-filed contracts from over 500 companies, spanning 22 years. These were executed agreements from some of the largest and most heavily lawyered companies in the world. The findings showed plenty of interesting trends and fun examples. Six in ten contracts contained drafting issues. Many were minor. But one in 40 was high-risk—defined as changing the meaning of an agreement in a substantially negative way for at least one party—and they were concentrated in provisions that decide who gets paid, who carries the liability, and what happens in a dispute. None of this is a matter of carelessness by lawyers so much as a consequence of the length, complexity, and disjointed nature of how these types of SEC-filed agreements are prepared and negotiated. In this context, mistakes are inevitable. But they don’t have to be. Every company, public or private, will eventually run its contracts through products like Spellbook that will not only spot errors and risks immediately but suggest fixes based on a company’s own agreement context and real-time market data. Issue Example: A loan cap written two different ways. A mining company's loan agreement set its borrowing limit at "One Million Five-Hundred Sixty Thousand Dollars," then printed the figure beside it as $1,750,000.00. The words and the number differ by $190,000, and the mismatch appears twice. If the borrower and lender ever disagree, the contract gives a court no clear answer, and $190,000 turns on who wins. Findings at a Glance This study should be treated as a proxy for how much humans miss. We kept our analysis deliberately narrow, counting only objective drafting mistakes we could verify from the document itself. We could not judge whether an agreement was signed out of policy, drifted off market, or if a company gave away more than it should, let alone what sits inside the millions of private contracts. These numbers should be thought of as the floor, not a full account of everything worth fixing in an agreement. blogs.content: Insights When a Business Reorganizes, Each Assignment Clause Decides Which Contracts Move An assignment clause decides which contracts move freely when a business reorganizes. See a sample clause, consent and merger rules, and a review table. by Harvey Team • Nov 3, 2026 An assignment clause says whether a party can transfer its rights or obligations under a contract to someone else, and on what terms. A restrictive version, often called an anti-assignment clause, requires the other party's consent or limits transfers to named exceptions. A change of control clause can extend that restriction to a sale of the party itself. When a business reorganizes, sells a unit, or raises money, those clauses decide which contracts go with the business. Take a hypothetical software company, OpCo, that's moving its payroll analytics product line into a new wholly owned subsidiary, NewCo. The move covers 240 contracts, including customer agreements, supplier contracts, inbound software licenses, and an office lease in San Jose. About a year later, an outside investor plans to buy 30% of NewCo, and a lender plans to extend a credit line secured by NewCo's receivables. Every company, contract count, and clause in this example is hypothetical. OpCo will transfer the contracts directly, so the reorganization is an assignment of contract rights and duties from OpCo to NewCo. The 240 contracts mix services, sales of goods, software licenses, and a lease, and each type follows its own rules. Results turn on each clause's wording and governing law, so counsel confirms each conclusion for the states involved. Sorting 240 contracts by hand means reading the same few clause types again and again. AI changes that step. Harvey's review tables, for example, pull each contract's assignment terms into columns counsel can check against the source, so lawyer time goes to the consents and judgment calls. A Sample Assignment Clause Shows the Six Phrases That Decide a Transfer OpCo's customer form, used in 160 of the 240 contracts, has a contract assignment clause like this hypothetical one, with its six key phrases numbered: "Neither party may assign this Agreement (1) , whether voluntarily, by operation of law (2) , or otherwise, without the other party's prior written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld (3) . Either party may assign this Agreement to an Affiliate, or to a successor to the business it relates to, on written notice and without consent (4) . A Change of Control of a party is deemed an assignment (5) . Any attempted assignment in breach of this Section is void (6) ." The table reads each numbered phrase against OpCo's move: Phrase What it can do What it means for OpCo (1) "Assign this Agreement" Reach rights, duties, or both, depending on how the governing law reads it The move delegates OpCo's duties, so the ban reaches it under either reading (2) "By operation of law" Pull a merger into the restriction, depending on the deal structure and the state Doesn't decide a direct transfer, but would matter if NewCo later merged (3) "Shall not be unreasonably withheld" Generally require a reasonable basis to refuse consent outside the carve-outs Matters only if NewCo falls outside the Affiliate carve-out (4) "To an Affiliate... on written notice" Move the contract without consent, if the assignee meets the defined term and notice follows the notice section Decides the reorganization for the 160 contracts on OpCo's form (5) "Change of Control... deemed an assignment" Treat an ownership change as a transfer, measured by the defined term Decides whether the later investment in NewCo counts (6) "Void" In some states, make a noncompliant transfer ineffective instead of a breach that leaves a damages claim Raises the cost of a missed notice or consent The other 80 contracts use different assignment language, so the rules behind each phrase matter. Under a deadline, counsel also has to decide which provisions in this contract, for this deal, get a second look first. Take a hypothetical request that lands at 3:00 p.m. on a Friday afternoon. The VP of Support wants the contract for an AI customer support platform signed by Monday, at $180,000 a year, billed annually in advance. The provider's paper comes in three parts: a master services agreement (MSA), an order form, and online terms the MSA pulls in by URL. The platform will read your support tickets, so it will hold your customers' names, email addresses, and order histories. We'll follow this request from Friday afternoon to Monday's signature. Harvey's First Pass Turns Three Documents Into Four Flags Against Your Playbook The three documents go through Contract Intelligence, Harvey's contract review AI . It checks each document against your team's standard positions, which Harvey can build from contracts you've already signed.Those positions live in your contract playbook , and clauses that no rule covers get flagged as well. In this example, four provisions come back flagged. The provider's right to train its models on customer data, its right to add subprocessors by updating a web page, and a 36-month auto-renewal each depart from your positions. The MSA's change-in-terms provision matches no rule at all, so it goes to counsel for manual review. It lets the provider update its online terms by posting them, and it makes those terms control in a conflict. Your playbook in this example accepts a 12-month cap for software subscriptions, so the provider's cap doesn't come back as a deviation. Counsel also checks precedent. In this example, two earlier AI tool agreements that process customer data closed with a separate, higher cap for data-protection breaches. Throughout my career, I’ve worked across Legal Operations, legal technology, contract lifecycle management, eBilling, procurement, and operational transformation. blogs.content: Week 35 · August 24–28, 2026 Copy page Copy page Resume terminal sessions in the Claude Code Desktop app, review feedback reports that Claude drafts for you, and start a session in restricted mode. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.240 → v2.1.250 3 features · August 24–28 Resume terminal sessions in the Desktop app Desktop Type /resume in the Claude Code Desktop prompt box to pick up any session you started from the CLI and continue it in the app with the full conversation and context intact. Search your sessions by title, folder, or branch, and preview where you left off before you resume. In a Desktop session, run the command to list your terminal sessions: Claude Code > /resume Select a session and press Enter . The conversation opens in the app where you left off. Move between the CLI and Desktop Claude-drafted feedback CLI When a tool keeps failing, Claude can’t help with a request, or you point out a mistake, Claude now drafts a feedback report for you with the SendFeedback tool. A card above your prompt shows the draft, and you can review, send, or dismiss it from there. Nothing reaches Anthropic until you send it. Requires v2.1.238 or later. Run /feedback with no argument to open your queue of drafts from every session: Claude Code > /feedback Select a draft, then edit, send, or discard it. To turn drafting off, set Claude-drafted feedback to off in /config . SendFeedback tool behavior Restricted mode v2.1.248 Restricted mode starts Claude Code without the built-in tools that run commands or code. Use it when an evaluation harness drives claude on a shared machine. Start it with --restricted or set CLAUDE_CODE_RESTRICTED=1 . blogs.title: AI 幻觉怎么发现？三个能被你抓到的破绽（附判断方法）
blogs.author: AutoClaw Team
blogs.description: 本文指出AI幻觉虽然难以根除，但是会留下三个可读出的文本破绽，数字干净得可疑、引用查无此物、从不说“不知道”。因此，我们可以依次检查，在查证前快速识别编造内容…
blogs.content: 返回博客 AI 幻觉怎么发现？三个能被你抓到的破绽（附判断方法） 资讯 作者：AutoClaw Team 2026年11月13日 本文指出AI幻觉虽然难以根除，但是会留下三个可读出的文本破绽，数字干净得可疑、引用查无此物、从不说“不知道”。因此，我们可以依次检查，在查证前快速识别编造内容，并把有可校验终点的活交给流程、判断与署名留给自己。 它错的时候，句子通常比对的还顺。 AI 幻觉是什么？指模型凭空生成不存在的信息。 它的机制不神秘：大模型做的是接着上文往下写，写出一段"最像答案"的文本——目标是"像"，不是"对"。所以幻觉不是故障，是这种工作方式的副产品。这类输出已经进了正式工作流：研报、纪要、合同、法律文书。而它没有可信度标记——一段编出来的话，和一段查证过的话，长得一模一样。幻觉消不掉。换更大的模型、接上检索，只能压低比例，压不到零。既然消不掉，剩下的问题就只有一个：怎么发现。 AI 编东西的时候，会留下三种它自己抹不掉的痕迹。你不需要查证任何资料，读的时候就能看见。查证是起疑之后的事。 本文多数时候就叫它"编"。 因为这个行为和人编假话没有区别：不是记错，是现造。至于怎么判断一段输出有没有编，看三个破绽就够。另外，"看得出"它对不对，是金融 AI 使用指南里的第三个条件，本文把"看得出"展开讲。 拦不住 的AI 幻觉：大模型幻觉检测的局限 拿到一段 AI 生成的内容，多数人的做法是通读一遍，凭感觉。这个做法有效：语病、常识错误、前后矛盾，读一遍基本能看出来。但 AI 编的东西恰恰没有语病，也不违反常识。它句子通顺、格式标准、语气笃定，读起来比不少人写的还顺。你凭感觉要找的那些毛病，它一个都没有。 所以不能只靠感觉，要看痕迹。下面三个破绽，按检查成本从低到高排：数字零秒，引用三十秒，语气要读完全文。 破绽一：数字干净得可疑 读的时候能看见什么。 精确到不合理的位数，比如"转化率提升 37.42%"；整数得反常，比如"市场规模恰好 500 亿"；通篇没有一个数字带口径、带取数时间。 数字为什么会露出毛边。 真实的数字是从系统里取出来的，身上带着三样东西：零头，因为业务不按整数发生；口径，因为同一个指标有不止一种算法；取数时间，因为数据每天在变。编出来的数字是"生成"的，生成器知道数字应该长什么样，不知道真实的数字具体是多少，于是给出一个光滑的结果。开头那个 99.8% 就是标准长相：精确、孤立、无处可查。当然，整数本身不是罪证——整数加上没有口径，才是。 起疑后 30 秒：问它数从哪来 挑一个最关键的数字，问它这个数是哪来的。答得出取数路径——哪张表、什么时间、什么口径——可以继续谈；答不出，或者只回一句"根据公开数据"，这个数字按不存在处理。 一个数字都不用查，留意位数和口径，怀疑就完成了。这是三个破绽里成本最低的一个。把活交出去时也一样。第二层叫"整理成表"，分水岭只有一条：来源敢不敢把取数路径摊开。 破绽二：AI 给的参考文献是假的，格式却完美 这类东西长什么样。 期刊名、卷号、页码一应俱全，作者名字听起来就是这个领域的人；但链接点不开，DOI 无效，按标题搜，查无此文。 它学的是引用长什么样，不是引用存不存在。 训练时它见过大量文献条目：期刊名配年份、作者配标题、卷号配页码。这套格式它学会了，哪份引用真的存在，它没有学会。所以生成的条目格式完美，指向虚无。 起疑后 30 秒：复制，搜一次 把它给过的任何一条出处原样复制，搜一次。三十秒以内出结果：搜得到，这一条过；搜不到，全文存疑。不是只有引用存疑，是全文。编引用和编数字是同一只手。这不是逻辑证明，是一条经验规则：一个来源在一个地方编，你在别的地方就得替它多花时间。 到这里，检查的代价从零秒涨到三十秒。下一个更贵。 破绽三：它从来不说"不知道" 一句话就能试出来。 你问什么它都有答案。陈述一件可查的事实时是这种语气，预测明年、评价一家名不见经传的公司、给一个业内有争议的口径下结论时，还是这种语气。该犹豫的地方，它一处都不犹豫。 这道防线怎么建，另一篇讲过。这里只讲一件事：它已经写完了，你怎么从字面上看出来。 为什么它没有"不知道"这个选项。 它被训练成"给出回答"，不被奖励"承认不知道"，至少在多数面向普通用户的产品里是这样。一个真正懂行的人知道边界在哪里：哪些问题有定论，哪些只有观点，哪些连数据都没有。一个从不说"不知道"的作者，不是因为全知道，是因为没有"不知道"这个选项。 AI 幻觉的典型表现：三个破绽一张表 三个破绽分别长什么样、起疑之后花多少时间验证，看这张表。手上有带小数点的数字，先看第一列；手上有引用，先看第二列；要判断这个来源还能不能信，看第三列。 破绽 怎么看出来 起疑后做什么 检查成本 数字干净得可疑 精确到不合理的位数；整数反常；无口径、无取数时间 挑一个数字问"哪来的"，看能否答出取数路径 零秒，读的时候留意 引用查无此物 格式完美；链接点不开；按标题搜不到 原样复制任意一条出处搜一次；搜不到则全文存疑 三十秒，一条一次 从不说"不知道" 问什么都有答案；该犹豫处不犹豫；语气全程一样确定 故意问一个不可能有答案的问题，看它编不编 读完全文才判得出 顺序不能反。先查引用再问语气，你会先花掉三十秒；先读语气再看数字，你会读完全文才发现第一句话的数就是编的。便宜的先做，做的过程里你会越来越不信它。这个"越来越不信"，比任何单个动作都有用。 换到季报点评上：AI 幻觉的三个破绽长什么样 换到金融，三个破绽更具体。 破绽一，在点评第一段。 "公司三季度营收 1,324.67 亿元，毛利率 28.35%，同比提升 1.2 个百分点。"精确到小数点后两位，看上去认真算过。但通篇没写含税不含税，没写是否追溯调整口径，没写哪一天取的数。麻烦在于同比增速照着这个数算，整篇自洽，读起来严丝合缝。抽三个数字——营收、毛利率、那个 1.2 个百分点——逐个问取数路径；答不出，全篇按待核处理。 破绽二，在行业对比那一段。 "据某券商 2026 年 7 月《XX 行业深度》，行业集中度已升至……"作者、标题、页码齐全，像翻过原文。复制标题搜一次，搜不到就是编的。动作只有一个：搜；搜不到，全文存疑。 破绽三，在你多问一句的时候。 "这家公司明年营收多少？"它给一个数，还带同比增速。明年的数还不存在，它答得和今年一样确定。此后它所有笃定的判断，都要降一级。 同一套动作，换到研报、招股书、投委会材料上 换场景，AI 幻觉的痕迹不变。研报摘要里那句"据某券商测算，2027 年渗透率将达 34.2%"，招股书摘录里的"行业规模 1,850 亿元"，投委会材料里的"可比公司平均毛利率 41.6%"——都按同一顺序过：先问口径，再搜一次出处，最后问一个明年才有的数。 三个动作，成本不到两分钟。省掉任何一个，签字的都是一份你自己复核不了的稿子。 AutoClaw 在这三处做了什么，没做什么 破绽一，靠的是每个数字能指回去。财报 PDF 的三张表，行名各家写法不同，"营业收入""营业总收入"混着来，第一步是把行名映射到同一套口径；映射错了，后面算出来的同比全是错的。这件事有唯一答案，跟原表一对就知道对不对。再往上一层，每个数字能指到哪张表、哪一行、什么时候取的——这是"整理成表"敢不敢交出去的硬前提。AutoClaw 的材料读取做的正是这一段：三张表和关键段落先读出来，口径对齐之后才谈同比。 破绽二，靠的是出处跟着稿子一起留下。引用不该只活在模型的回答里：你点一下，看到的是原文那一页，不是它复述的一句话。定时交付把初稿送到你手上的时候，出处跟着一起走，你不用另外去翻。这一步做到，"搜一次"才从动作变成习惯。 破绽三，能做的只有一件：没数据时说没有。 AutoClaw 的位置画在这条线上：取数、整理、成稿、按时交付，这些有可校验终点的交给流程；假设成不成立、结论敢不敢署名，留给签字的人。参数和结果留下来方便复核，但留痕不是核验，核验是你签字前的最后一步。 工具能做到成稿，做不到签字。放到金融的日常里，AI 幻觉出现的地方很具体：季报点评、定期跟踪、同业对比，这三类活有可校验的终点——数字指得回原表、出处点得开、没数据时它说没有。终点之前的交给 AutoClaw，终点之后的交给你。三种活里，最容易被当成"随便写写"的是季报点评，最容易出事也是它，因为它看起来最像有人认真算过。 AI 幻觉识别失效的五种情况 它改写你亲手给的材料时，不灵。 数字是你喂的，出处是你给的，三个破绽一个都不会出现。这时候要核对的是它有没有改错你的数字，那是另一套防法。 逻辑层面的错，不灵。 每一步都对、结论不成立，把同时发生当成因为所以，这是判断问题，不是痕迹问题，只能靠你的专业。 源头数据本身就错，不灵。 上游数据有误，它照实引用，错得"有据可查"，三个破绽全部失效。 前三条是它管不到的。下面两条不一样，那不是管不到，是用反了。 用另一个 AI 来检测，别。 检测器自己也是模型，同样会编。开头那个自称准确率 99.8% 的工具就是证据：它用来证明自己可靠的数字，恰恰符合本文教你的第一个破绽。我后来没点进去。真要用检测器，看三件事：样本量、测试集是什么内容、方法是否公开。三个都没有，那个数字按不存在处理。 接了检索，不等于不编。 检索能压住一部分凭空生成，压不住"取回来了但读错""引用了但张冠李戴"。上面那份实测测的正是带检索的产品。 AI 幻觉怎么发现，答案不在“更准的检测”里，在“能被你抓住的痕迹”里。 三个破绽有一个共同点——它们都长在文本表面，不需要你手上有任何外部资料：数字精确到可疑、出处查不到、什么都答得出来。这也是它比检测工

Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.220 → v2.1.224 3 features · August 3–7 Cross-session messaging v2.1.224 Your Claude Code sessions can now message each other. Claude discovers your other sessions with the ListAgents tool and sends with SendMessage , either when you ask it to or on its own, such as after a change in one session affects what another is working on. A message is text Claude writes for the other session, never your conversation history or files. Available on macOS and Linux. Requires v2.1.224 or later. With two sessions open on the same machine, ask one of them to pass something along: Claude Code Tell the session working on the payments API that users.name is now users.display_name The other session shows a Message from row once Claude has read the message; press Ctrl+O to expand it. Message another session Self-hosted environments v2.1.224 Self-hosted environments run Claude Code cloud sessions on your organization’s own infrastructure, in public beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Run claude self-hosted-runner on your machines or containers to turn them into runners. When someone picks your environment while starting a session from claude.ai, the mobile or desktop apps, or claude --cloud , that session runs inside your network, with access to your internal services. An Owner turns on Allow self-hosted environments in admin settings first. Signed in as an Owner, run the guided setup, which walks you through creating the environment and starts a runner: terminal claude self-hosted-runner setup The environment shows Healthy in admin settings once the runner registers. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.214 → v2.1.219 3 features · July 20–24 Claude Opus 5 new model Claude Opus 5 is the new default Opus model in Claude Code. It’s the default on Max, Team Premium, Enterprise pay-as-you-go, and the Anthropic API, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Cloud’s Agent Platform. On the Anthropic API and on Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, Opus 5 runs with a 1M-token context window ; on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, select the 1M model variant. Fast mode moves to Opus 5 at $10/$50 per MTok. Requires v2.1.219 or later. Switch to Opus 5 by name, or pick it from the model picker: Claude Code > /model claude-opus-5 Model configuration iOS Simulator in Claude Code Desktop Desktop Claude Code Desktop on macOS gets an iOS Simulator pane, in public beta on Pro, Max, and Team plans. When Claude builds, launches, or checks your app in a simulator, the pane opens next to the conversation and streams the device screen live, so you can watch Claude tap through the app to verify its changes or drive the device yourself. Requires Xcode with the iOS platform installed, and Claude Desktop v1.24012.0 or later. Ask Claude to run or test your app, and the pane opens when the app launches: Claude Code > Build the app and run it in the simulator to check the onboarding flow. Test iOS apps in the simulator Claude Security plugin plugin The Claude Security plugin runs a multi-agent vulnerability scan of your codebase inside a Claude Code session: agents map your architecture, build a threat model, hunt for vulnerabilities, and independently review every finding before writing the report to a CLAUDE-SECURITY-<timestamp>/ directory. Scan a whole repository or only a branch’s diff, a pull request, or a single commit, then turn the findings you choose into reviewed patches that you apply yourself. Install the plugin from the official Anthropic marketplace, run /reload-plugins , then start a scan with /claude-security : Claude Code > /plugin install claude-security@claude-plugins-official Scan and fix your codebase Other wins /code-review now runs as a background subagent with its own context window, so review work stays out of your conversation and the findings arrive when it completes /verify , /code-review , and /deep-research run only when you invoke them; Claude no longer launches them on its own Emoji shortcodes autocomplete in the prompt input: type :heart: to insert an emoji, or two or more characters after : for suggestions; turn it off with emojiCompletionEnabled Skills with context: fork run in the background by default, and background: false in the skill’s frontmatter waits for the result in the same turn A session runs up to 20 subagents concurrently by default; change the limit with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS --max-budget-usd now enforces the cap on subagents: once spend reaches it, Claude can’t start more and running background subagents stop New sandbox.filesystem.disabled setting skips filesystem isolation while keeping network egress control In auto mode, the checks for dangerous rm commands, background jobs, and suspicious Windows paths no longer open permission dialogs; the auto-mode classifier adjudicates them instead Bash permission checks fail closed on more shell forms, including file-descriptor redirects, Zsh variable subscripts in [[ ]] comparisons, help and man invocations that could run unsafe options, and commands over 10,000 characters Fast mode no longer supports Opus 4.7: /fast now applies to Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 Long-running tool calls emit a periodic progress heartbeat instead of going silent Full changelog for v2.1.214–v2.1.219 → Was this page helpful? blogs.description: 一、民商事诉讼从证据梳理到庭后归档环环相扣，本文按办案的真实顺序，介绍 AutoClaw 法律助手在每个环节能交付什么。 二、证据梳理、策略与风险评估、法律检索、争…
blogs.content: 返回博客 从接案到归档：AutoClaw 法律助手在诉讼中的应用 资讯 作者：AutoClaw Team 2026年11月13日 一、民商事诉讼从证据梳理到庭后归档环环相扣，本文按办案的真实顺序，介绍 AutoClaw 法律助手在每个环节能交付什么。 二、证据梳理、策略与风险评估、法律检索、争点归纳、文书起草、判决摘要与脱敏归档，每一步都有可溯源、可核验的成果。 三、各环节的材料和成果在同一个项目里累积，后一步直接承接前一步，律师可以把精力留给需要专业判断的地方。 代理律师在一起诉讼案件里的工作复杂而繁重：接手之初要从数百页聊天记录、往来邮件和证据材料中理出时间线；起诉前要确定请求权基础，检索研判法条与类案；庭前要逐字打磨每一份文书，归纳争议焦点、预演对方抗辩；庭后还要完成上诉评估、案件复盘与归档。这些工作环环相扣，任何一处疏漏都可能影响案件质量。 智谱 AutoClaw 法律助手是面向法律工作的 Agent，用简单的提示词就能围绕具体的法律任务直接产出可交付的成果，像一位随时在场、每条结论都标明出处的助理。目前它已经能参与诉讼案件的办理，覆盖法律检索、案件材料整理、文书生成、合同审查、文件脱敏等工作。 一、能力纵览 AutoClaw 法律助手基本覆盖诉讼全流程：从接到案卷、梳理事实，到分析策略、预演攻防，再到文书成稿、结案复盘，每一步的产出都可以溯源、核验。 更重要的是，这些步骤不是彼此隔离的。材料与成果都留在同一个项目里，每个阶段都在同一套底稿上推进，中途不需要重新整理；哪个环节走到哪一步、还缺什么，随时可查，全案可以统筹推进。 下文从民商事律师的实务工作切入，按办案顺序逐一介绍。文中截图使用的是一起虚构的股权回购案和一起虚构的民间借贷案。 二、功能介绍 1. 证据梳理 整理客户提供的原始材料、梳理案件时间线和具体事实，是办理诉讼案件的必经环节。 这项工作从证据的电子化与识别开始。收到扫描件、聊天记录截图、沟通录音等原始材料后，律师可以直接把它们上传到 AutoClaw 项目。法律助手会逐份解析，识别其中的内容，让每份材料带着来源和时间归入案卷；遇到大文件会提示处理方式。接案当天就能进入事实梳理。 在此基础上，一句简单的指令就能生成时间线与事实底稿：每个事实节点都标注出处，事实与证据的对应关系直接可查；能证明的事实、单方陈述和待补强的事实分开列示，不会混在一起。律师如果有惯用的工作模板，也可以一并上传，AutoClaw 会按这套格式组织时间线和事实梳理文档。以截图中的股权回购案为例，法律助手读完 22 份材料（其中包括 10 张微信截图），整理出交易结构、全案时间线和 7 项待核实事项。 识别矛盾与瑕疵，是证据梳理中最耗时的环节：合同约定的付款比例和对账单对不上，聊天里提到的交付日期和验收报告差了半个月，流水里某笔款项的备注与用途存疑。法律助手会比对主体、时间、金额，把有出入的地方直接列给律师。上面的案例里，它发现客户的回购函按 10% 计算了全程利息，而《补充协议》约定自 2023 年 6 月 10 日起才调至 10%，分段计算会少约 73.2 万元，诉请金额需要律师决策。 梳理完成后，法律助手同步编制证据目录：逐项编号，标注每份证据的名称、来源与待证事实，并检查证据链是否闭环，缺了哪一环、该往哪个方向补，都写在目录之后。这份目录一次编制、全程使用：后续凡需引用证据都从它出发，不必反复翻检原始材料；全案证据的状况也清楚可见，取证与举证可以提前安排。 2. 策略制定与风险评估 诉讼请求的确定是全案策略的起点。请求权基础选错方向，后续的检索与举证都会落空。 在这一步，法律助手提供的是决策参照。综合检索报告把各条候选请求路径涉及的法条、司法解释、类案裁判倾向和立法背景放在一起呈现，附适用条件与风险提示；不同路径的构成要件、举证负担与裁判支持度可以并排比较，诉讼请求的取舍有据可依。同时，它会对诉讼时效、管辖、举证责任分配、财产保全等事项逐项提示，每项风险都附应对方向，便于在起诉前补强。 制定策略的另一个关键是预判对方的做法。只需输入“换成被告视角再检索”，法律助手就会从对方立场预演抗辩路径，己方的举证重心随之倒推确定。抗辩预演不再依赖律师一个人逐一穷举，也更不容易遗漏。 3. 法律检索与类案研究 诉讼策略要落到条文与案例上，就需要检索。检索结果是否可靠，取决于三件事：数据从哪里来、怎么检索、最后交付什么。AutoClaw 法律助手在这三处都有针对性的设计。 数据来源：多个专业数据源打底 法律助手接入了华宇元典、北大法宝、法天使、天眼查和见微数据等专业数据源，每个数据源负责不同的工作：华宇元典用于检索裁判文书、类案结果、争议焦点和裁判理由，为诉讼策略研判提供依据；北大法宝覆盖法律法规、司法解释、裁判案例、专题资料和法学观点，是规范检索的主要来源；法天使提供专业合同模板库，覆盖劳动、租赁、购销等常见合同类型，起草和审查合同时可以直接调用；天眼查可以查询企业工商信息、股权结构、实际控制人、关联关系和司法风险，确定诉讼主体、排查财产线索时都能用上；见微数据用于检索企业公告、事件、政策和行业动态，处理涉及上市公司的案件时，可以在对话里直接核对公告和舆情，不用另开窗口；另外还接入了美国、欧盟、日本、中国香港等境外官方法律数据源，为涉外工作助力…… 各数据源合计收录约 42,700 部法律法规、148 万条法条、7,860 万篇裁判文书（2010—2025 年）和 2,953 万篇行政处罚决定书（2000—2026 年），案例与法条之间的引用关系约 4.8 亿条。最新政策、法答网答问、司法解释征求意见稿、地方裁判口径这类时效性强的内容，数据库可能还没收录，法律助手会先联网检索找到线索，再与数据库交叉核验后引用。已有自有数据库账号的律师，也可以在连接器里完成授权后直接使用，目前支持北大法宝、华宇元典、企查查、天眼查、法研等。 检索技能与提示词模板：按法律工作方法分类，自动调用 除了数据源，法律助手还配备了一套按法律工作方法组织的专业技能（Skill），提交任务后由它自动调用，不需要记任何指令。这些技能对应检索由浅入深的几层需求：只想核实某个条号的原文、某份规范的效力状态，单点法律速查会用最短路径给出答案；想把一个问题研究透彻，综合法律检索报告会把法条、司法解释、裁判倾向与立法背景系统铺开，并逐项校验规范是否现行有效、层级有无冲突；检索类案，有专门的技能沿相似事实与裁判规则展开，并区分法院层级与地区差异；立法背景、地方指导意见、会议纪要、行业标准等外围信息，以及“对赌协议”“借名买房”这类生活用语的法律含义，也各有技能补足。 类案检索用自然语言提问即可，不需要专门设计检索式。不想自己组织问法时，也可以点选法律助手内置的检索提示词模板：模板按场景预置了检索指令，点选后自动填入输入框，补充案情后发送即可。 交付成果：一份可以直接归档的检索报告 一次检索结束后，法律助手交付的是一份分层组织的报告，可以直接归入案件项目，作为工作底稿使用。 报告先给出检索问题对应的结论，归纳这类案件的主流裁判做法和常见分歧；接着列出具体依据，法条给出编号、原文与现行效力，类案逐案呈现法院层级、裁判要旨及与本案的异同，不同层级、不同地区法院的裁判口径差异也一并归纳，管辖评估与和解空间判断都建立在同一批可溯源的类案上；风险与例外单独列示，结尾写明实务路径。截图中的民间借贷类案检索报告共 21 页，纳入 10 件近五年类案，其中 5 件调取了裁判文书全文逐字核验。 4. 争议点归纳 庭审攻防围绕争议焦点展开。庭前需要把双方主张拆解为一项项具体的争议点，并配上事实、证据与法律依据。争点归纳的水平，直接决定庭审的攻防质量。 法律助手会从案卷中提取争点，按请求权基础逐一展开，每项争点都附对应的证据与法律依据。在争点之下，它逐项评估证据的三性与证明力，给出补强建议；论证按“事实要件、法律要件、结论”组织成链，尚未覆盖的缺口直接标出，开庭前该补哪些论证清清楚楚。股权回购案中，法律助手归纳出 4 项核心争点和 5 项次级争点，并为每项标注了风险等级。 当律师援引的规则存在记忆偏差或容易混淆时，法律助手不会简单回答“不存在该规定”，而是辨析混淆的来源，指出可能是哪个相似但适用对象不同的制度。一位试用过的执业律师评价：“不仅给出了明确意见，还进行了延伸思考，指出问题可能涉及到的问题，有举一反三的效果。” 5. 诉前准备与文书起草 诉讼文书伴随案件全程，从起诉到结案，每个环节都有对应的文书。文书各有体例，硬要求却一致：结构规范，案情真实。 无论起草起诉状、答辩状还是代理词，当事人名称、合同编号、金额、日期等关键信息都取自项目里已上传、已分析的文件，不会凭空生成；事实部分可以直接溯源到证据目录。起草过程中，法律助手同步读取证据材料、调用法条检索逐项核对，文书援引的每一条规范都有出处；整个执行过程在面板中全程可见，每一步都能展开查看。 可起草的文书覆盖诉讼各环节：起诉状开启诉讼，答辩状逐项回应，代理词归纳攻防，申请书处理程序事项，另有律师函、法律备忘录和客户说明。同一份文书可以分别形成初稿、客户可读版与内部分析版，读者不同，侧重也不同。行文遵循律师的文书习惯：结论先行、依据清楚、有适用性分析、风险例外明确、实务路径可执行。 AutoClaw 法律助手还提供 Word 和 WPS 插件，安装后可以直接在文档里起草和打磨文书。在侧边面板发出起草指令，文书就地生成，不必在对话窗口与文档之间来回搬运；修改同样就地完成，改动以修订痕迹落在正文，可在审阅中逐条接受或拒绝，每处修改都附批注说明问题与理由，并标注风险等级。 6. 判决书

  • Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do

  • Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions

  • Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
  • Fixed /schedule leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
  • Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
  • Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block

blogs.content: Week 25 · June 15–19, 2026 Copy page Copy page Publish a live, shareable page from your session with Artifacts, match tool parameters in deny and ask rules, and set any setting from the prompt with /config. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.178 → v2.1.183 3 features · June 15–19 Artifacts An artifact is a live, interactive page that Claude Code publishes from your session to a private URL on claude.ai, and it updates in place as the session keeps working. Ask for one when terminal text is the wrong medium, such as a PR walkthrough with the diff annotated inline or a dashboard built from session data. Artifacts are in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Ask Claude for a page, then approve the publish prompt: Claude Code Make an artifact that walks through this PR with the diff annotated inline. Create an artifact Match by input parameter v2.1.178 Deny and ask permission rules can now match a tool’s input parameters with the Tool(param:value) syntax. For example, Agent(model:opus) matches subagent spawns that request the Opus model tier. The value accepts * as a wildcard, so Agent(isolation:*) matches any explicit isolation value. Add a parameter rule to the deny list in settings.json : .claude/settings.json { "permissions" : { "deny" : [ "Agent(model:opus)" ] } } Match by input parameter Set any setting from the prompt v2.1.181 Pass key=value to /config to change a setting directly without opening the Settings interface. The syntax also works in non-interactive mode with the -p flag and from Remote Control. Set the thinking setting from the prompt: Claude Code /config thinking=false Commands reference Other wins Auto mode now blocks destructive git commands ( git reset --hard , git clean -fd , git stash drop ) when you didn’t ask to discard local work, and blocks terraform destroy unless you asked for the specific stack Set the new attribution.sessionUrl setting to false to omit the claude.ai session link from commits and PRs in web and Remote Control sessions In the /config interface, Enter and Space both change the selected setting, and Esc now saves and closes instead of reverting New sandbox.allowAppleEvents opt-in setting lets sandboxed commands send Apple Events on macOS Point CLAUDE_CLIENT_PRESENCE_FILE at a marker file to suppress mobile push notifications while you’re at the machine Long paragraphs now stream line by line instead of waiting for the first line break API connection drops mid-thinking now retry automatically instead of showing “Connection closed while thinking” With CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 set, every session has one implicit team, so you spawn teammates directly with the Agent tool’s name parameter Skills in nested .claude/skills directories load when working on files there; on a name clash the nested skill appears as <dir>:<name> so both stay available Fixed prompt caching not reading on a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and on Microsoft Foundry Fixed Write and Edit producing zero-byte or truncated files on network drives and cloud-synced folders Full changelog for v2.1.178–v2.1.183 → Was this page helpful? This page is the reference for the Code tab. The sidebar lists your sessions and lets you run several in parallel. blogs.content: Week 24 · June 8–12, 2026 Copy page Copy page Move a session to a new directory with /cd, let subagents spawn their own subagents, and troubleshoot a broken configuration with safe mode. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.166 → v2.1.176 3 features · June 8–12 Move a session with /cd v2.1.169 The new /cd command moves the current session to a different working directory without rebuilding the prompt cache: the new directory’s CLAUDE.md is appended as a message instead of replacing the system prompt. The session relocates to the new directory’s project storage, so --resume and --continue find it there. Claude prompts you to trust the directory if you haven’t worked in it before. Move the session into another project without restarting: Claude Code > /cd ../other-project Commands reference Subagents can spawn subagents v2.1.172 Subagents can now spawn their own subagents. The subagent panel below the prompt shows the full tree: each row carries a count of its descendants and a path back to main . Subagent chains are capped at five levels deep to prevent runaway concurrent trees. Open the agents view to watch the nested tree as work fans out: Claude Code > /agents Spawn nested subagents Troubleshoot with safe mode v2.1.169 Start Claude Code with --safe-mode , or set CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE , to launch with all customizations disabled: CLAUDE.md , skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, and custom commands and agents do not load. Authentication, model selection, built-in tools, and permissions still work. If a problem disappears in safe mode, one of those surfaces is the cause. Launch a clean session to isolate a broken configuration: terminal claude --safe-mode Test against a clean configuration Other wins fallbackModel configures up to three fallback models tried in order when the primary is overloaded or unavailable, and --fallback-model now applies to interactive sessions too Session titles are now generated in the language of your conversation; pin a specific one with the language setting claude agents --json adds --all to include completed sessions plus new id and state fields, and no longer omits blocked or newly dispatched sessions Browsing a marketplace’s plugins in /plugin now has a search bar New disableBundledSkills setting and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BUNDLED_SKILLS hide bundled skills, workflows, and built-in commands from the model Deny rules accept a glob in the tool-name position, so ”*” denies all tools, and unknown tool names in deny rules now warn at startup Agent messaging is hardened: messages relayed via SendMessage from other agents no longer carry user authority, and auto mode blocks them Amazon Bedrock reads the AWS region from ~/.aws config files when AWS_REGION is unset, and /status shows where the region came from New enforceAvailableModels managed setting makes the availableModels allowlist also constrain the Default model Claude in Chrome browser tools now load in a single batched call instead of one per tool claude update announces the target version before downloading instead of going silent New footerLinksRegexes setting adds regex-matched link badges to the footer row Full changelog for v2.1.166–v2.1.176 → Was this page helpful? Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.158 → v2.1.165 4 features · June 1–5 Auto mode on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry v2.1.158 Auto mode is now available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry for Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.8, replacing permission prompts with background safety checks on third-party providers. Opt in by setting CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_AUTO_MODE=1 . Opt in on a third-party provider, then cycle to auto mode with Shift+Tab: terminal export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_AUTO_MODE = 1 Auto mode on third-party providers Safer automatic edits v2.1.160 Claude Code now prompts before writing files that can run code, even in acceptEdits mode. The protected set covers shell startup files such as .zshenv and .bash_login , git config under ~/.config/git/ , and build-tool configs such as .npmrc , .bazelrc , and .pre-commit-config.yaml . These writes are never auto-approved in any mode except bypassPermissions . Work in acceptEdits mode; Claude now pauses before writing these files: terminal claude --permission-mode acceptEdits Protected paths List installed plugins with /plugin list v2.1.163 The new /plugin list command prints your installed plugins inline, without opening the /plugin menu, and is also available as claude plugin list from the shell. In the interactive form, add --enabled or --disabled to show only plugins in that state. List the plugins that are currently turned on: Claude Code > /plugin list --enabled Plugin commands Version requirements for managed deployments v2.1.163 Two managed settings, requiredMinimumVersion and requiredMaximumVersion , let your organization require an approved Claude Code version range. A client outside the range exits at startup and tells the user to update through the organization’s method. claude update , claude install , and claude doctor keep working so users can still recover. Add a floor to your managed settings so older clients refuse to start: managed-settings.json { "requiredMinimumVersion" : "2.1.163" } Decide what to enforce Other wins The trigger keyword for dynamic workflows changed from workflow to ultracode ; asking for a workflow in your own words still works, and the keyword is highlighted in violet in the prompt Stop and SubagentStop hooks can return hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext to give Claude feedback and keep the turn going instead of being treated as an error claude mcp list, get, and add no longer print secrets: environment-variable references are not expanded, and credential headers and URL secrets are redacted A failed Bash command in a parallel tool batch no longer cancels the others; each tool returns its own result independently Editing a file no longer needs a separate Read first when you viewed it with a single-file grep , egrep , or fgrep Clicking a command in the autocomplete menu now fills it into your prompt instead of running it immediately; press Enter to run Listing Grep or Glob in --tools now provides the dedicated search tools on native builds with embedded search, instead of silently ignoring those names /effort now confirms when your chosen level will persist as the default for new sessions OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES values are now attached as labels on metric datapoints, so you can slice usage metrics by custom dimensions like team or repo Windsurf is renamed to Devin Desktop in /ide , /terminal-setup , and /scroll-speed , following the editor’s rebrand /btw gains a c to copy shortcut that copies the raw markdown answer to the clipboard Full changelog for v2.1.158–v2.1.165 → Was this page helpful?
